Idioms.phrase: Keep the ball rolling - To keep something going or to make sure it continues.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Could you please keep the ball rolling on this project for me while I'm away on vacation? If you could, I'd appreciate it!

Idioms.phrase: Keep up with - To match someone else in terms of progress or success.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Moira was careful to try to keep up with her co-workers’ achievements.

Idioms.phrase: Keep you posted - To keep someone notified of what is happening.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I'll keep you posted on what happens with the situation.

Idioms.phrase: Keep your chin up - To keep a positive and optimistic frame of mind.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I know things have been difficult lately but you've got to keep your chin up! Things will get better soon.

Idioms.phrase: Keep your head - Maintain your sense of logic and be sensible.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I told her it's essential that she keep her head when dealing with all this stress. It will be difficult, but it's necessary.

Idioms.phrase: Keep your mouth shut - Stay quiet about something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I need you to keep your mouth shut about this situation. Don't tell anyone about it.

Idioms.phrase: Keep your nose clean - Behave well and stay out of trouble.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, From now on, you need to stay out of trouble. Keep your nose clean.

Idioms.phrase: Keep your wits about you - Stay aware of the situation you are in and be ready to react if you need to.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I advised them to keep their wits about them when walking through that area. It can be quite dangerous.

Idioms.phrase: Keeping up with the Joneses - To try to keep up with other people in terms of wealth and material possessions.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I feel sorry for that family. They spent so much money just trying to keep up with the Joneses, and now they're in a lot of debt. How silly of them to think that they needed to copy their neighbor and have three sports cars!

Idioms.phrase: Kept in the dark - To be kept unaware of something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They kept me in the dark about their real plans for the trip. I thought that was very unfair, as I deserved to know the details.

Idioms.phrase: Keyed up - To be tense and anxious, perhaps in anticipation of something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Justin was a bit keyed up yesterday. He has an interview coming up soon, and he really needs this job.

Idioms.phrase: Kick up your heels – Celebrate.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Mia and Ava decided they would have a good time this weekend. They wanted to celebrate, really kick up their heels!

Idioms.phrase: Kill the mood - To do something that ruins someone else’s mood.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We were having a fun time at the party until Margaret arrived. She really killed the mood.

Idioms.phrase: Kill two birds with one stone - To accomplish two tasks with one action.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Elizabeth decided to run another errand while she was in the area. By doing so, she killed two birds with one stone.

Idioms.phrase: Kit and caboodle - Everything, or all things, involved in something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Wow! You packed a lot of luggage for this trip. You seem to have packed the whole kit and caboodle!

Idioms.phrase: Knee-jerk reaction - An automatic, unthinking reaction.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I wish Walter would think more about how he responds to things. He always seems to give a knee-jerk reaction.

Idioms.phrase: Knee-high to a grasshopper - Extremely young and small.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, My grandfather said he was knee-high to a grasshopper when he started to learn how to ride a bike.

Idioms.phrase: Knock into a cocked hat - Something that is made useless or debunked.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The scientist knocked their theory into a cocked hat. He totally disproved it.

Idioms.phrase: Knock it off - Stop it.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Knock it off! You're being too silly.

Idioms.phrase: Knock on wood - To tap your knuckle on wood in an effort to avoid bad luck.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I hope the roof stays okay for the remainder of the winter. Knock on wood!

Idioms.phrase: Knock someone's socks off - To surprise and impress someone.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Your presentation knocked our socks off! Everyone was talking about it afterward.

Idioms.phrase: Know the ins and outs - To have a detailed understanding of something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, It didn't take long to train her. She seemed to know all the ins and outs of the job within a couple of weeks.

Idioms.phrase: Know the ropes - To understand what to do and how to do it.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They made sure the new hire was trained by someone who really knew the ropes in the department.

Idioms.phrase: Know which way the wind is blowing - To comprehend a situation (generally negative).
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I was thinking about applying to work at that company, but I wanted to wait and see which way the wind was blowing. It seems to be in trouble.

Idioms.phrase: Know your onions - To be extremely knowledgeable on a topic.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, He's an expert on this topic. Without question, he knows his onions!

Idioms.phrase: Know zip - To know nothing.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, He knows zip on the subject. There's no need to consider his opinion.

Idioms.phrase: Knuckle under - To give in or be defeated.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Unfortunately, Ryan ended up knuckling under with all the pressure. He gave in before the contest was even over.

Idioms.phrase: Labor of love - Something one loves to do, especially for the benefit of someone one loves.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Don't worry about all the time I spent knitting this sweater. It was a labor of love.

Idioms.phrase: Laid off - To lose one's job.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, James found out that he is getting laid off from his job. He's really worried, as he won't have an income and will have to look for a new position.

Idioms.phrase: Lap of luxury - To be in an extremely luxurious situation.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The Smith family is extremely wealthy and lives in the lap of luxury. They have a mansion and two summer homes.

Idioms.phrase: Last but not least - Something that is saved for last, but is not necessarily less important than whatever has come before it.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We're having a delicious dinner tonight. And, last but not least, we're going to enjoy some lovely ice cream.

Idioms.phrase: Last straw - The latest problem in a series of problems. Something that leads someone to finally lose their patience.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Mr. Johnson said that Tom's sloppy work this past week was the last straw. He was going to be fired.

Idioms.phrase: Last-ditch effort - A final, perhaps desperate, effort at something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, He decided to make a last-ditch effort to fix the web site. He didn't know if he'd be successful, but he was going to give it his best shot.

Idioms.phrase: Laugh all the way to the bank - To gain money, most likely in a dishonest manner, and to feel smug about it.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, No wonder the owner of that fraudulent company is so happy. He must be laughing all the way to the bank.

Idioms.phrase: Lay an egg - To do something that is embarrassing.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I'm afraid I'll lay an egg during the play tomorrow. I just hope I get my lines right.

Idioms.phrase: Lay down the law - To set rules, probably strict ones.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The parents decided they needed to lay down the law when their kids misbehaved too badly.

Idioms.phrase: Lead someone around by the nose - To compel someone to do something, especially through manipulation or bullying.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We don't like the way that she leads all her friends around by the nose. She's always bossing them around and telling them what to do.

Idioms.phrase: Learn by rote - To memorize something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, In the past, students tended to have to learn most things by rote.

Idioms.phrase: Learn the ropes - To learn how to do something—especially, to learn how to do well in a new job
Idioms.definition: As in this example, It will take a while for the new trainees to learn the ropes and become full employees.

Idioms.phrase: Learned my lesson - To have learned from an experience, probably one caused by a mistake.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Noah learned his lesson about planning ahead when he ran out of time to study for his test.

Idioms.phrase: Leave me alone - I want to be alone, so please stop talking to me; please go somewhere else, somewhere out of my sight.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Look, please just leave me alone. I don't want to talk about this right now.

Idioms.phrase: Leave no stone unturned - To look in every possible place.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I promise that I'll leave no stone unturned while looking for that book you want.

Idioms.phrase: Leave someone high and dry - To leave someone in a difficult position and to take things away from them.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They left him high and dry. It was extremely unfair for them to treat him like that.

Idioms.phrase: Leave well enough alone – Don’t involve yourself in a situation that already seems stable and decent enough.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Don’t bother her with that tonight. Leave well enough alone.

Idioms.phrase: Left me in the lurch - To be left in a difficult situation.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I was left in the lurch by my co-workers the other day. They left the entire remainder of the work to me.

Idioms.phrase: Left out in the cold - Left out of something pleasant, or excluded from an opportunity.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, He wanted to invest in the endeavor but was left out in the cold. He couldn't find the opportunity.

Idioms.phrase: Left someone behind - To leave someone somewhere and to go somewhere else.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The group of teenagers acted unpleasantly toward their friend. They even left her behind when they decided to go downtown.

Idioms.phrase: Lend me your ear - Please listen to me.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, If you'd lend me your ear for a few moments, I'd like to play my newest song for you.

Idioms.phrase: Lend someone a hand - To help someone.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Lauren gave Debbie a hand with her homework. She often helped her in this way.

Idioms.phrase: Let bygones be bygones - Leave past grievances in the past.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, James and Jonathan had argued a lot in the past, but they decided to let bygones be bygones and to focus on the future.

Idioms.phrase: Let sleeping dogs lie - Stop talking about an issue.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Jessica told me that she still wants to try to address the issue with Molly. But I said it might be better to let sleeping dogs lie.

Idioms.phrase: Let someone off the hook - To refrain from holding someone accountable for something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, He was angry that his friend was late returning his book, but he let him off the hook.

Idioms.phrase: Let the cat out of the bag - To reveal a secret.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The release date for the book remained a secret for a long time, but someone finally let the cat out of the bag.

Idioms.phrase: Let the dust settle - To wait for circumstances to return to normal after something significant has happened.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Brad's family has just had a major crisis and they're still recovering. I told him to try to wait for the dust to settle before he makes any major decisions.

Idioms.phrase: Let your hair down - Let yourself relax.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Don't worry about all the things you need to do tomorrow. Just let your hair down and enjoy yourself.

Idioms.phrase: Letter perfect - Precisely correct.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Everything she does is letter perfect. She's a great student and does wonderfully on her tests.

Idioms.phrase: Level playing field - Fair and even circumstances, especially when it comes to anything with an element of competition.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I feel that there should be a level playing field in school. Teachers and others should make an effort to ensure that all students have the things they need to succeed.

Idioms.phrase: Life of Riley - A very comfortable, and probably luxurious, life.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They won the lottery last year. That's why they can live the life of Riley now.

Idioms.phrase: Light of my life - Someone you love who makes your life more cheerful and that you like to be around.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Brenda said that her daughter is the light of her life. She is always talking about her.

Idioms.phrase: Like a chicken with its head cut off - To behave in a frenzied manner.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Marcie acted like a chicken with its head cut off when she heard the news. She got really anxious and ran around in a panic!

Idioms.phrase: Like a deer in headlights - To have a stunned or confused look on one's face.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, He looked like a deer in headlights when they confronted him about the money.

Idioms.phrase: Like clockwork - On a very regular basis.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The event happened every other Friday night, like clockwork.

Idioms.phrase: Like nailing jello to the wall - A very difficult or impossible task.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Figuring out what we should do was really difficult. It was like nailing jello to the wall.

Idioms.phrase: Like pulling teeth - Extremely difficult; often refers to a difficulty in getting someone to do something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Trying to make the store manager realize that I deserved a refund was like pulling teeth. I was there for half an hour!

Idioms.phrase: Like riding a bicycle - Something you never forget, or stop knowing, how to do.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, She was worried that she wouldn't remember how to solve the problem. However, she soon realized that it was a bit like riding a bike. You never forget.

Idioms.phrase: Like taking candy from a baby - Extremely easy to do, especially something that involves convincing someone to do, or to give, something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Convincing Paul to give me the information I needed was easy. It was like taking candy from a baby.

Idioms.phrase: Like there is no tomorrow - Living in the moment.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They went from store to store yesterday, shopping as if there was no tomorrow.

Idioms.phrase: Like water off a duck's back - It doesn't bother me.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The other students thought they were bothering me with their teasing. They didn't realize it was like water off a duck's back.

Idioms.phrase: Live and learn - I will learn from a mistake that I have made.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I made a huge mistake the other day. But live and learn.

Idioms.phrase: Live and let live - To be non-judgmental of others.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I believe in everyone living the way that they feel is best for them. Live and let live!

Idioms.phrase: Live it up - Have lots of fun.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I think it's time to live it up this weekend. We've been working so hard.

Idioms.phrase: Living the dream - Living a wonderful life, the type one would dream of.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I asked how they felt after they won the lottery. They said they're living the dream!

Idioms.phrase: Lock, stock, and barrel - Absolutely everything involved.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Can you believe it? They thought they were going to take everything, lock, stock, and barrel!

Idioms.phrase: Long face - A sad facial expression.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Why the long face? I thought you felt happy now.

Idioms.phrase: Long in the tooth - Older or elderly.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Bill has been feeling a bit long in the tooth lately. He thinks he's old now.

Idioms.phrase: Long time no see! - I haven't seen you in a long time.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Long time no see! I think we last saw each other a couple of years ago.

Idioms.phrase: Look before you leap - Think carefully before acting or taking a risk.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Look before you leap! You don't want to leave your job for a new one without first thinking it out properly.

Idioms.phrase: Look like a million bucks/dollars - To look very attractive, usually well-dressed.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Tricia took three hours to get ready for the dance. Her family told her she looked like a million bucks!

Idioms.phrase: Look like the cat that swallowed the canary/got the cream - To look smugly pleased or satisfied with oneself.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Kathryn was so pleased with herself. She looked like the cat that swallowed the canary!

Idioms.phrase: Loose cannon - A person who is unpredictable and difficult to control, and who will probably inadvertently cause problems.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Everyone in the office thought that David was a loose cannon. He was extremely unpredictable and seemed likely to cause problems.

Idioms.phrase: Lose one's shirt - To lose a large amount of money, probably one’s financial security as a whole.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The businesspeople ended up losing their shirt on the new venture. It was a disaster.

Idioms.phrase: Lose touch - To discontinue contact with someone, often unintentionally.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The two friends lost touch over the years. They no longer exchanged letters or holiday cards.

Idioms.phrase: Lose your marbles - To go crazy.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, He was quite rude about his friend. He said that he thought that he'd lost his marbles and couldn’t think rationally anymore.

Idioms.phrase: Lose your touch - To lose one’s ability or skill in a specific area.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I was worried that I might have lost my touch when I failed to convince my friend of something the other day. I've always been so good at persuading people.

Idioms.phrase: Lost at sea - To feel confused about a situation, and to not know what to do.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, He said he feels lost at sea right now. He can't decide what path to take.

Idioms.phrase: Lost my head - To become overcome with emotion or anger; to act irrationally.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I'm afraid I lost my head the other day when I found out about my friend's betrayal. The news shocked me.

Idioms.phrase: Low-hanging fruit - Something that is easy to take advantage of.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, It turned out that they saw me as low-hanging fruit. They thought they could take advantage of my kindness.

Idioms.phrase: Luck out - To be very lucky.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, She lucked out when she won $1,000 on a scratch card.

Idioms.phrase: Lucky break - Something very lucky has happened.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The actress got a lucky break when she found a way to get to the audition and then won the part.

Idioms.phrase: Lucky dog - A lucky person.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, You lucky dog! I can't believe you won that sports car!

Idioms.phrase: Mad as a hornet - Crazy or frantic.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, He's as mad as a hornet! Did you see the way he was acting? It was crazy.

Idioms.phrase: Made for each other - When a couple is extremely well-suited to each other.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The couple has so much in common that people say they are made for each other.

Idioms.phrase: Made my hair stand on end - To be very frightened.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The horror movie was terrifying! It made my hair stand on end.

Idioms.phrase: Make a beeline for - To go directly toward.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Whenever his friend comes over, he always makes a beeline for his video game system! They enjoy playing together.

Idioms.phrase: Make a big stink - To complain loudly.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The customer made a big stink when he complained about the bad quality of the product.

Idioms.phrase: Make a long story short - To recount something in a brief way, leaving out unnecessary details.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Yes, we plan to go there again. To make a long story short, we had an amazing time!

Idioms.phrase: Make a mountain out of a molehill - To exaggerate about the significance or severity of circumstances.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Sabrina was really overreacting. She was making a mountain out of a molehill.

Idioms.phrase: Make a pit stop - To stop somewhere for a short period of time, usually during a long journey.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We made a lot of pit stops on the road trip, to go to the bathroom and to eat.

Idioms.phrase: Make a scene - To create a fuss of some kind that draws the attention of others in a negative way.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Stop talking so loudly! I know you're upset, but you are making a scene. People are looking.

Idioms.phrase: Make ends meet - To have enough money for daily expenses over the course of a month.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Kim was finding it difficult to make ends meet because of her limited income.

Idioms.phrase: Make eyes at someone - To look at someone in a flirtatious way.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, She was making eyes at the guy she had a crush on all evening.
